assignments.value: # Werkstudent Data Engineering: German job market intelligence report  **The German market for Werkstudent Data Engineering positions is small but accessible — roughly 60–120 unique openings exist nationally at any given time, with the candidate's Python/SQL/Docker profile matching the core requirements of the vast majority of postings.** The broader addressable market, including adjacent roles like Data Science, Backend Development, and Analytics, expands to 300–600 positions. However, the junior-level IT market is tightening: unfilled IT positions have dropped from 149,000 (2023) to 109,000 (Bitkom, August 2025), and GenAI adoption is correlated with reduced junior hiring while increasing senior demand (SSRN #5425555, February 2026). For a candidate based in Siegen with no cloud or big data framework experience, the realistic strategy centers on targeting the Köln–Frankfurt commuting corridor and remote-friendly consulting firms, while investing 10–15 hours in Azure and Airflow basics to close the most impactful perceived gaps.  ---  ## Section 1: A niche market of 60–120 postings with strong adjacent overflow  The national posting volume for "Werkstudent Data Engineering" sits at approximately **60–120 unique positions** after deduplication across portals. Indeed.de displays roughly 100 results for the broad search term and 25–32 for the exact title "Werkstudent Data Engineer" (Indeed.de, April 2026). LinkedIn shows **64 postings** for "Werkstudent Data Engineer (m/w/d)" filtered to Germany (LinkedIn.de, April 2026). StepStone returns 1,456 results for "Werkstudent in Data Engineering," but this figure is inflated by broad keyword matching that captures tangentially related IT Werkstudent postings; the actual exact-match count is estimated at 50–120. Campusjäger/Workwise, a curated student platform, shows an estimated 5–15 active listings based on individual search results visible, though it does not publish aggregate counts.  Adjacent roles significantly expand the addressable market. Indeed.de shows approximately **200 postings** for Werkstudent Data Science, **273** for Werkstudent Softwareentwicklung, **141** for Werkstudent Backend, **100** for Werkstudent Data Analytics, **50–80** for Werkstudent Business Intelligence, **52** for Werkstudent Big Data, and fewer than **10** each for Werkstudent ETL and Werkstudent MLOps (Indeed.de, April 2026). The term "Werkstudent Python" returns 592–664 results, but this reflects Python appearing as a skill keyword across many unrelated role types rather than a distinct job category. "Werkstudent Informatik" — the broadest CS umbrella — shows roughly **3,479** listings on Indeed and 3,595 on Glassdoor, providing context for the overall Werkstudent IT market.  The **Werkstudent-to-Praktikum ratio** for Data Engineering is approximately **1.3:1**. Indeed shows ~100 Werkstudent versus ~71–81 Praktikum Data Engineering postings. The Data Science ratio is wider at roughly 1.8:1, suggesting Data Science more strongly favors the ongoing Werkstudent model. For portal selection, **Indeed.de provides the most granular and filterable results** with reliable count displays. LinkedIn and Glassdoor report the highest raw volumes (32,000–34,000 total Werkstudent jobs in Germany) but suffer from heavy aggregation and broad matching. StepStone is useful for breadth but not precision. Campusjäger/Workwise offers fewer but more curated, student-specific listings.  Seasonal patterns follow the German academic calendar closely. **Peak hiring occurs in February–April** (for summer semester positions starting in April) and **July–September** (for winter semester positions starting in October). Bosch's career portal recommends applying 4+ months before the desired start date; Karrierebibel advises 3–6 months lead time due to competition. The current timing of April 2026 aligns with the end of the spring hiring peak — many summer semester positions have been filled, but rolling and mid-semester postings remain active. The **next optimal application window opens in July–September 2026** for winter semester starts. A hiring trough typically occurs November–January during the holiday season and budget-cycle closings.  ---  ## Section 2: Köln and Frankfurt are the commutable sweet spots from Siegen  The highest concentration of Werkstudent Data Engineering postings clusters in **Berlin (25–65+ estimated postings), München (20–40+), and Hamburg (15–30)** based on cross-referencing StepStone, Indeed, and Glassdoor location filters. StepStone explicitly lists Berlin, Hamburg, and München as the top three cities. Among NRW cities, **Köln holds 10–25 estimated postings** with employers like REWE Group, niologic, and Ströer SE; **Düsseldorf shows 8–15** with ERGO and Kienbaum; **Bonn has 5–10** including Deutsche Post/DHL and Comma Soft. Frankfurt, driven by the finance sector, holds an estimated 10–20 postings with Ströer SE, VR-Payment, and consulting firms. Stuttgart (10–20, dominated by Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, and TRUMPF) and Nürnberg (5–10) round out the secondary tier.  From Siegen, commuting viability varies dramatically. **Köln is the strongest commuting option** at 1 hour 25 minutes by direct RE9 train with 20+ daily connections, costing only €49/month via the Deutschlandticket (Deutsche Bahn). **Frankfurt is equally viable** at 1 hour 25–33 minutes via direct HLB trains running every two hours. Bonn requires one change and takes approximately 1 hour 32 minutes — marginal for 2–3 days per week. Düsseldorf at roughly 1 hour 48 minutes with one change and Dortmund at approximately 1 hour 50 minutes are difficult for regular commuting but possible once or twice weekly. Stuttgart (3+ hours), Hamburg (5+ hours), Berlin (5+ hours), and München (5+ hours) are **not commutable and require either relocation or fully remote arrangements** (Deutsche Bahn, Omio, Trainline estimates).  Remote and hybrid availability is meaningful but not dominant. An Indeed search for "Remote Data Werkstudent" returns **75 postings** nationally; Glassdoor shows **288 "Work from Home Werkstudent"** positions. Analysis of individual postings suggests approximately **10–15% offer fully remote work**, **40–50% offer hybrid arrangements** with phrases like "Home Office möglich" or "mobiles Arbeiten," **25–30% prefer on-site with occasional flexibility**, and **10–15% are strictly on-site**. Berlin is the most remote-friendly region; Munich and Stuttgart are the most on-site-focused, particularly in the automotive sector where Mercedes-Benz postings state "Du solltest nahe am Einsatzort wohnen." Consulting firms like Senacor Technologies explicitly state that employees can work "von jedem Ort im DACH-Raum" thanks to hybrid models.  Language requirements present a manageable barrier for this candidate. Approximately **70–80% of postings require German at B2 or above**, with typical phrasing like "Deutsch auf C-Niveau (verhandlungssicher)" or "mind. B2" (Porsche, TRUMPF, DIGITIUM, MAN, Infineon postings). The candidate's C1 German comfortably meets this threshold. Berlin stands out with **367 English-only working student jobs** (Glassdoor) and many postings where "German is a plus but not required." Köln is mixed — niologic posts in English while DIGITIUM requires German B2. Munich and Stuttgart overwhelmingly require German.  The single most important employer to target is **adesso SE**, which has an office in Siegen itself, offers "Homeoffice möglich," and actively posts Data Engineering Werkstudent roles across its 10+ NRW locations. Other high-priority employers include **REWE Group** (Köln, 102+ Data Engineer roles on StepStone), **Ströer SE** (Köln/Frankfurt, Data Lake/Databricks focus with home office), **Senacor Technologies** (hybrid from anywhere in DACH), and **Deloitte** (multi-location with AI & Data delivery teams in Leipzig, Frankfurt, and other cities).  ---  ## Section 3: Expect €15–18 per hour, with a hard floor at €14.50  No salary database publishes specific hourly rates for "Werkstudent Data Engineering" as a standalone category. Gehalt.de does not have a dedicated page for this role, Kununu provides no specific salary data, and Ratbacher and Bitkom reports focus on full-time positions. The analysis below draws from the closest available proxy data.  The **German minimum wage (Mindestlohn) as of January 1, 2026 is €13.90/hour** (BMAS/Bundesregierung), rising to a planned €14.60 in 2027. This sets the legal absolute floor. General Werkstudent rates across all fields center on a **median of €16/hour** (Glassdoor, n=6,844, March 2026) with P25 at €15 and P75 at €17–18. Indeed reports an NRW-specific average of **€16.38/hour** across all Werkstudent roles (Indeed.de, March 2026). Werkstudent Informatik specifically averages **€14.72/hour** across 439 companies surveyed by Berufsstart.de (2025), while Glassdoor's IT Werkstudent category shows a median of **€16/hour** (n=12) — a discrepancy likely explained by Berufsstart reporting advertised rates versus Glassdoor's employee-reported actual pay. Werkstudent Data Science on Glassdoor shows **€14–19/hour** with a €16 median (n=10), and Software Engineer Working Student shows **€14–23/hour** with a €16 median (n=271).  **At the Werkstudent level, the "Data Engineering" label does not reliably command a premium** over general IT Werkstudent roles. The premium manifests at the full-time level (Data Engineers earn ~€70–80k versus ~€55k for general IT), but for working students, the employer type and sector matter far more than the role title. Sector-specific data from MLP Financify (2025) shows **insurance at €15.84/hour**, energy at €15.55, finance at €14.25, IT at €14.10, and automotive at €13.82. IGM-tarifgebunden companies (IG Metall union-bound) typically pay **€16–20/hour** regardless of degree level (WiWi-TReFF forum reports). Anecdotal reports place BMW Data Analytics at €25/hour (Master level, Munich), Siemens at €15.70–19.37/hour, Deutsche Bahn at €16–20/hour, and typical Köln IT startups at €15/hour.  The Bachelor-versus-Master differential is **€1–3/hour** at companies with flexible pay scales but **zero at many large IGM companies** that use fixed Werkstudent rates. The candidate's 5th semester and strong GPA of 1.8 (top ~15%) partially offset the Bachelor-stage discount. Being in Siegen, a non-hub city, means local roles will sit at the lower end of NRW ranges.  For this specific profile, the **negotiation floor should be €14.50–15.00/hour** — accepting less would be below-market for an Informatik B.Sc. student with a strong GPA and documented projects, and should only be considered for an exceptionally valuable learning opportunity. The **realistic target range is €15–17/hour for Siegen-local or NRW hybrid roles** and **€16–19/hour for remote positions with larger-city employers**. The **realistic ceiling without cloud or Spark experience is approximately €20/hour**, achievable at IGM Konzerne, banks, or insurers. Rates above €20/hour are rare for Bachelor students and typically reserved for Master-level candidates at premium employers.  ---  ## Section 4: 16 role types ranked from most to least aligned  The following table covers every relevant role type the candidate might encounter, ordered by alignment with a Data Engineering career path. Posting frequency estimates are based on Indeed.de and LinkedIn April 2026 data.  **Werkstudent Data Engineering** — Posting frequency: medium-low (~60–120). Bridge quality: strong (direct target). The core role itself, with typical requirements of Python, SQL, ETL pipeline development, and data modeling. Tech stack overlap with the candidate is excellent across Python, SQL, PostgreSQL, Docker, Git, and ETL concepts via n8n.  **Werkstudent ETL Developer** — Posting frequency: rare (<10). Bridge quality: strong (direct equivalent). Nearly always labeled as Data Engineering instead. Tasks are identical — building extraction, transformation, and loading pipelines. The candidate's n8n orchestration experience maps directly.  **Werkstudent Analytics Engineer** — Posting frequency: rare (<10). Bridge quality: strong. An emerging role focused on SQL transformations, dbt, and data modeling. Extremely well-aligned with the candidate's SQL and PostgreSQL strengths, though dbt knowledge would help.  **Werkstudent Big Data** — Posting frequency: rare (<15). Bridge quality: strong. Usually combined with Data Engineering in practice. May require Spark/Hadoop exposure, which the candidate lacks, but the Python and SQL foundation transfers directly.  **Werkstudent MLOps / ML Engineering** — Posting frequency: low (~15–30). Bridge quality: strong. Combines pipeline engineering with ML model deployment. The candidate's Docker, Python, and LLM API integration experience is highly relevant. Small candidate pool means less competition.  **Praktikum Data Engineering** — Posting frequency: medium-low (~71–81). Bridge quality: strong (direct). Same technical requirements as Werkstudent but structured as a 3–6 month full-time internship. Large companies like Mercedes-Benz and BMW sometimes prefer this format.  **Werkstudent Backend Development** — Posting frequency: medium-high (~141). Bridge quality: strong. Software engineering with significant data overlap, often involving Python/Django/FastAPI, REST APIs, and database work. The candidate's NestJS, REST API, and PostgreSQL experience aligns well.  **Werkstudent Python Developer** — Posting frequency: medium-low (~30–60). Bridge quality: strong. General Python development roles that often include data processing, automation, and API work. The candidate's Python stack is a near-perfect fit.  **Werkstudent KI / AI Engineering** — Posting frequency: low-medium (~20–40). Bridge quality: strong. An emerging category where the candidate's RAG pipeline and LLM API integration experience serves as a rare differentiator that few Werkstudent applicants possess.  **Werkstudent Datenbank / Database** — Posting frequency: low (~15–25). Bridge quality: strong. PostgreSQL and SQL expertise map directly. These roles tend to be more operational (DB administration) than pipeline-focused.  **Werkstudent Data Science** — Posting frequency: medium-high (~200). Bridge quality: moderate-to-strong. More ML and statistics-focused than Data Engineering but shares Python/SQL foundations. The candidate's ML certifications and LLM experience are relevant. Higher competition due to more postings and more applicants.  **Werkstudent DevOps** — Posting frequency: medium-low (~40–70). Bridge quality: moderate. Docker, CI/CD, and infrastructure automation overlap is strong, but the role is less data-specific. Good for building cloud and infrastructure skills the candidate currently lacks.  **Werkstudent Software Engineering** — Posting frequency: high (~273+). Bridge quality: moderate. The broadest category with the highest volume. May involve non-data work (frontend, mobile), but the candidate's full-stack skills (NestJS, Angular, TypeScript) make this a viable fallback with many openings.  **Werkstudent Automatisierung / Automation** — Posting frequency: medium-low (~30–50). Bridge quality: moderate. Variable content — may involve manufacturing RPA or software automation. Python-focused automation roles align well with the candidate's web scraping and workflow orchestration experience.  **Werkstudent Data Analyst** — Posting frequency: medium-high (~100–250). Bridge quality: moderate. High volume but lower technical bar, focused on dashboards, reporting, and SQL queries rather than pipeline engineering. Good fallback, though the candidate may find it less technically challenging.  **Werkstudent Business Intelligence** — Posting frequency: medium (~50–80). Bridge quality: weak-to-moderate. Heavily focused on Power BI, Tableau, and SAP — tools the candidate does not currently know. The SQL overlap exists but the role trajectory diverges from Data Engineering.  ---  ## Section 5: SQL and Python are non-negotiable, cloud is aspirational  Analysis of 18+ actual Werkstudent Data Engineering job postings from Indeed, StepStone, LinkedIn, Glassdoor, and company career pages (including jovoco, Deloitte, TRUMPF, Schwarz IT, MTU Aero Engines, Infineon, niologic, Mercedes-Benz) reveals clear skill tiers.  Skills appearing in **70%+ of postings** (must-haves): **SQL** appears in approximately 95% of all postings, making it the single most universal requirement. **Python** follows at 85–90%, often with explicit mention of Pandas and PySpark. Being an **enrolled CS or related student** is a structural requirement in ~95% of Werkstudent postings. **German language at C1+** is required in 70–80% of postings, though Berlin is more lenient. **ETL/ELT concepts** — described as "Datenpipelines," "ETL-/ELT-Pipelines," or "Datenverarbeitungsstrecken" — appear in roughly 70% of postings as required understanding or core tasks.  Skills appearing in **30–60% of postings** (differentiators): **Cloud platforms (AWS/Azure/GCP)** are mentioned in 40–50% of postings but almost always as "wünschenswert" (desirable) rather than hard requirements for Werkstudent roles. Azure dominates the German enterprise market. **Power BI or BI visualization tools** appear in 40–50% of postings, particularly in hybrid DE/Analytics roles. **Git and version control** show up in 35–50% of listings. **Data modeling and data warehouse concepts** appear in 35–45%. **English language proficiency** is mentioned in approximately 50% of postings. **Pandas and data libraries** are explicitly named in 30–40%. **Databricks** appears in 25–35%, especially at consulting firms like EY and Deloitte.  Skills appearing in **fewer than 30% of postings** (nice-to-haves): Apache Spark/PySpark at 20–30%, Docker at 20–30%, dbt at 15–25%, CI/CD at 15–25%, Apache Airflow at 10–15%, Snowflake at 15–20%, REST APIs at 15–20%, Apache Kafka at 5–10%, Scala/Java at 10–15%, and Infrastructure as Code at fewer than 10%.  The candidate's profile covers the must-have tier comprehensively. **Python with Pandas, SQL, PostgreSQL, Git, and ETL concepts through n8n** satisfy the core requirements. Among differentiating skills, Docker and Docker Compose set the candidate apart from most B.Sc. Werkstudent applicants who typically know only Python and SQL. The **RAG pipeline and LLM API integration experience is the candidate's strongest differentiator** — very few Werkstudent candidates possess hands-on AI/LLM skills, and a growing number of postings (Mercedes-Benz GenAI, Cassini KI & Data, niologic AI Systems) explicitly seek these capabilities.  The most impactful skill gaps, ranked by frequency as requirements: **(1) Power BI / BI tools** at 40–50% mention rate, often as a soft requirement for hybrid DE/Analytics roles; **(2) Cloud platforms** at 40–50% mention rate, almost always nice-to-have for Werkstudent; **(3) Databricks** at 25–35%, nice-to-have; **(4) Apache Spark** at 20–30%, nice-to-have; **(5) dbt** at 15–25%, nice-to-have and growing; **(6) Apache Airflow** at 10–15%, partially mitigated by n8n experience; **(7) Apache Kafka** at 5–10%, negligible for Werkstudent roles.  ---  ## Section 6: Every major gap is a nice-to-have, not a gatekeeper  **Cloud platforms (AWS/GCP/Azure):** Mentioned in 40–50% of Werkstudent Data Engineering postings, but the phrasing is consistently permissive — "wünschenswert," "Interesse an Cloud-Technologien," or "Erste Erfahrung oder Studienkenntnisse" (jovoco, Deloitte, TRUMPF postings). Only at Big4 consulting firms does cloud approach a firmer expectation, and even Deloitte's posting states "Interesse an Software Engineering & Cloud-Technologien (egal ob AWS, Azure oder GCP)" — interest, not expertise. Candidates without cloud experience are **regularly hired** for Werkstudent positions; companies expect to train students in their specific stack. Honest framing: the candidate should emphasize Docker and Docker Compose experience as a foundation for containerized cloud deployments and express concrete learning intent. **Acquiring surface-level knowledge meaningfully changes the candidate's position** — completing the free Azure Fundamentals (AZ-900) learning path (~6 hours on Microsoft Learn) would allow honest listing of "Grundkenntnisse in Azure" and help pass keyword filters. Azure is recommended over AWS for the German enterprise market.  **Apache Spark:** Appears in 20–30% of postings, virtually **never as a hard requirement** for Werkstudent roles. Typical phrasing: "PySpark wünschenswert" (TRUMPF), "Interesse an Datenplattformen, Apache Spark" (Deloitte). The vast majority of Werkstudent Data Engineering hires have never used Spark. Honest framing: emphasize Python/Pandas data processing experience as the conceptual foundation that Spark scales horizontally. Surface-level knowledge via a Databricks Community Edition PySpark tutorial (~4–6 hours) provides moderate benefit but is lower priority than cloud.  **Apache Kafka:** Mentioned in only 5–10% of Werkstudent postings and **never as a hard requirement** at the student level. Kafka is primarily relevant for senior roles involving real-time streaming architectures. Virtually all Werkstudent hires have no Kafka experience. No special framing needed — the candidate should not proactively address this gap unless a specific posting mentions it. Surface-level learning provides minimal benefit.  **Apache Airflow:** Appears in 10–15% of Werkstudent postings, almost always as nice-to-have. This is the gap where the candidate has the strongest mitigation story: **n8n is a genuine workflow orchestration tool**, and the core concepts — DAGs, scheduling, dependency management, error handling — are transferable. Honest framing: "Ich habe praktische Erfahrung mit Workflow-Orchestrierung durch n8n, wo ich ETL-Pipelines und automatisierte Datenverarbeitungsprozesse aufgebaut habe. Die Kernkonzepte sind direkt auf Apache Airflow übertragbar." Running a basic Airflow tutorial in Docker (~2–4 hours, leveraging existing Docker skills) would allow honest listing of Airflow basics and is **highly recommended** as a medium-priority investment.  **No professional experience:** Many postings include "Erste praktische Erfahrungen" but this is understood in the Werkstudent context — **these positions are designed for students without extensive industry experience**. The candidate's four documented Data Engineering and automation projects serve as credible evidence of practical capability. Framing should emphasize project outcomes, technical decisions made, and problems solved rather than professional tenure.  **Prioritized upskilling by ROI:** (1) Azure Fundamentals AZ-900, ~6 hours, free — highest impact; (2) Power BI basics via Microsoft Learn, ~8–10 hours, free — addresses second most common gap; (3) Apache Airflow Docker tutorial, ~3 hours — combines with existing n8n narrative; (4) dbt Fundamentals online course, ~4 hours, free — positions for modern data stack roles; (5) PySpark via Databricks Community Edition, ~4–6 hours — lowest priority for Werkstudent applications.  ---  ## Section 7: A tightening junior market with a 6-month window of opportunity  The Werkstudent Data Engineering market is **transitioning from a candidate's market to a more balanced, increasingly employer's market for junior and student-level roles**, while remaining candidate-favorable relative to non-IT fields. Bitkom's August 2025 survey of 855 companies reports **109,000 unfilled IT positions nationally** — a significant decline from the 2023 peak of 149,000 and the 2022 figure of 137,000 (Bitkom Presseinformation, August 7, 2025). The Hays Fachkräfte-Index IT dropped to **59% in Q4 2025**, reaching 2020 levels after peaking at higher values in 2022–2023 (Hays Q4/2025). IT job postings declined approximately **26% year-over-year** in 2024 versus 2023 (IW Köln analysis). Despite this softening, 85% of companies still report IT skills shortages and 79% expect the shortage to worsen (Bitkom, 2025).  The critical nuance for this candidate is the **junior versus senior split**. A study of 285,000 companies (published SSRN, February 2026) found that GenAI adoption correlates with increasing hiring of senior roles but **decreasing hiring of junior roles**. Bitkom data confirms the trend: 27% of companies plan to cut jobs through AI, while 42% say AI will create additional IT roles — but the net effect disproportionately affects entry-level positions. Get-in-it.de's 2026 analysis summarizes the situation as "good long-term perspectives, but noticeably higher competitive pressure at entry level."  Estimated **application-to-interview conversion rates for well-matched Werkstudent Data Engineering candidates sit at 15–25%** (medium confidence — no systematic studies exist for this specific segment). A LinkedIn case study from a data analytics job seeker in Germany reported a 22% application-to-first-interview rate and an overall 1.96% application-to-offer rate, requiring roughly 51 applications per offer (Pavel Kukushkin, LinkedIn, 2020). The niche nature of Data Engineering — with fewer postings but also fewer qualified applicants compared to Data Science — likely yields somewhat better conversion rates. SmartRecruiters reports a median German time-to-hire of **55 days** for general positions, 45% above the global average, partly due to Betriebsrat involvement. For Werkstudent positions specifically, the process is typically faster: **3–8 weeks** from application to decision, with large companies (Siemens, BMW) taking 4–8 weeks and smaller firms responding within 1–2 weeks (WiWi-TReFF forum reports, Karrierebibel). Total time from application to start date, including semester alignment, ranges from **4–12 weeks**.  Selectivity is **clearly increasing** compared to 12 months ago. The Hays IT index fell from roughly 79% in Q2 2025 to 59% in Q4 2025, open IT positions dropped by 40,000 in two years, and IT job postings declined 26% year-over-year. However, data engineering demand specifically remains robust — the BLS/aichanging.work projects **+36% job growth for data engineers through 2034**, and a Coalesce 2026 report notes that "76% of data work is now enhanced by AI tools," with AI's complementary impact "significantly outweighing its substitution effect."  Several structural factors will shape the next six months. The **EU AI Act's high-risk system obligations become fully enforceable on August 2, 2026** — AI used in recruitment is classified as high-risk, requiring documentation, human oversight, and bias testing, with fines up to €35 million or 7% of global revenue for non-compliance. This creates **positive demand for data engineers** who can implement AI governance, data quality frameworks, and compliance infrastructure. The German economy is expected to grow **+0.8% to +1.7% in 2026** (ifo: +0.8%, IW Köln: ~+1.0%, DIW: +1.7%), recovering from near-stagnation. The ITK market is growing **+4.4% to €245.1 billion** with AI platform revenues doubling annually (Bitkom). Government fiscal stimulus of **€38 billion planned for 2026** should support the second half of the year. Counterbalancing these positives, US tariff impacts are dampening German growth by an estimated 0.6 percentage points (ifo), and the broader economic weakness means companies are hiring "with the handbrake applied" (Hays characterization).  The candidate's optimal strategy given current timing: apply aggressively now to remaining spring-cycle openings and rolling positions, then prepare a concentrated application push in **July–September 2026** for winter semester starts. The July–October Semesterferien period, during which Werkstudent employees can work up to 35–40 hours per week, makes candidates who start before the lecture-free period particularly attractive to employers. SECTION 1 — ROLE AND TASK CONTEXT
You are a precision career data extraction engine operating inside a 
multi-node automated pipeline. Your output feeds directly into downstream 
processing nodes — errors here propagate silently through the entire system. 
Accuracy and strict schema compliance are not optional.

SECTION 2 — CRITICAL RULES [read these first, they apply to every field]
RULE 1: Return ONLY a valid JSON object. No preamble, no explanation, no 
        markdown fences, no text outside the JSON.
RULE 2: Do NOT infer, assume, or extrapolate beyond what is explicitly 
        stated in the four input sources (<cv_text>, <technology_list>, 
        <city_list>, <career_target>).
RULE 3: skill_gaps qualifiers MUST use ONLY these two formulas:
        — "no hands-on experience"
        — "no hands-on experience (has used [X] in the same domain)"
        NEVER write: "conceptual foundation", "transferable knowledge", 
        "provides a basis", "similar background", or any other variation.
RULE 4: role_type_scores MUST contain EXACTLY ONE value of 12. No exceptions.
RULE 5: role_type_scores MUST always include both closing entries as keys:
        "Other adjacent IT" and "Unrelated (sales, legal, manual, etc.)".
RULE 6: A technology present anywhere in <cv_text> — under any heading, 
        with any proficiency qualifier (including "grundlegend", "basic", 
        "familiar") — is NOT a gap. Mention = presence. 
        Do not apply judgment about proficiency level.
RULE 7: role_type_scores keys must be derived by reading <role_list> 
        role labels and immediately stripping any contract-type word 
        (Werkstudent, Praktikum, Freelance, Minijob, Vollzeit → remove).
        Perform this strip BEFORE writing any key.
        If stripping two different labels produces the same key, merge them 
        into one key and keep the higher score.

SECTION 3 — DETAILED INSTRUCTIONS

=== BLOCK A: candidate_profile ===

Execute in this exact order:

Step A1 — name
Extract the candidate's full name from <cv_text>.

Step A2 — core_skills
<core_skills_list> contains pre-computed technologies ordered by 
frequency of appearance in the CV's projects.
Include only items from <core_skills_list> that also appear in 
<technology_list>. Copy names exactly. Comma-separated.

Step A3 — secondary_tools
List tools and platforms that appear in <cv_text> but do not qualify 
for core_skills under the rules above.
Comma-separated.

Step A4 — skill_gaps

Sub-step 1 — START FROM LIST: <technology_list> contains every 
technology extracted from the market research. This is your complete 
starting list. Do not add or remove items at this stage.

Sub-step 2 — FILTER: For each technology in <technology_list>,
search <cv_text> for that exact string.
  — If found anywhere in <cv_text> (any heading, any qualifier): REMOVE it.
  — If NOT found: keep it and assign qualifier:
      a) If no related tool in the same category appears in <cv_text>:
         → "no hands-on experience"
      b) If a different tool solving the same problem appears in <cv_text>:
         → "no hands-on experience (has used [cv_tool] in the same domain)"

  Category examples for qualifier (b):
  — Web frameworks (e.g. Django, FastAPI, Flask, Express.js, NestJS, 
    Spring) are the same category.
  — Data processing libraries (e.g. Pandas, PySpark, Spark) are the 
    same category.
  — Workflow orchestration tools (e.g. Airflow, Prefect, Luigi) are the 
    same category.
  — Cloud data warehouses (e.g. Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) are NOT 
    the same category as relational databases (e.g. PostgreSQL, MySQL).
  — Cloud platforms (e.g. AWS, Azure, GCP) are NOT the same category 
    as containerization tools (e.g. Docker, Kubernetes).

  When searching, also accept common name variants: a full name 
  ("Apache Kafka") matches a short name ("Kafka") and vice versa.
  If uncertain whether two names refer to the same tool, treat as 
  match and REMOVE.

Sub-step 3 — ASSEMBLE: Build the skill_gaps array from what remains.

Step A5 — home_location
Extract city and region from <cv_text> only. Do not infer from 
university name, phone prefix, or any other indirect signal.

Step A6 — commute_options

Sub-step 1 — START FROM LIST: <city_list> contains every city 
extracted from the market research. This is your complete city list.
Do not add or remove cities at this stage.

Sub-step 2 — CALCULATE: For each city in <city_list>, calculate 
approximate train travel time from home_location.
Use only travel times explicitly stated in <market_research>.
If <market_research> provides a range, use the midpoint rounded 
to the nearest 5 minutes.
If <market_research> does not state an exact time for a city, 
use your best estimate and format as:
"City (~approx. Xh by train)" — the word "approx." goes 
immediately after the tilde, before the time value.

Format each entry as:
  "City (~Xh by train)"
  "City (~Xh Xmin by train)"
  If travel time is under 1 hour: "City (~0h Xmin by train)"
  If the city is the home city: "City (~0h, home city)"
  Flag as "occasional-only" ONLY if travel time is STRICTLY GREATER 
  than 2 hours: "City (~Xh by train, occasional-only)"
  A city at exactly 2h does NOT receive the flag.

Sub-step 3 — ASSEMBLE: Join all entries with " | ".
The home city entry must always appear first.

Step A7 — target_format
Extract desired work arrangement and weekly hours from <cv_text> or 
<career_target>.

=== BLOCK B: role_type_scores ===

<role_list> contains every pre-extracted role with its label, 
frequency, and bridge_quality. Use it as your only source for 
deriving keys. Do not read <market_research> for role derivation.

Step B1 — KEY DERIVATION FROM role_list

Sub-step 1 — STRIP: For each entry in <role_list>, remove any 
contract-type word from the label:
(Werkstudent, Praktikum, Freelance, Minijob, Vollzeit → remove)
This is your candidate key.

Sub-step 2 — MERGE: If stripping two different labels produces 
the same candidate key, keep only one key and assign it the 
higher of the two scores calculated in B2.

Sub-step 3 — FREQUENCY FILTER: Keep a candidate key only if its 
frequency maps to INCLUDE per this table:
  "very high"    → INCLUDE
  "high"         → INCLUDE
  "medium-high"  → INCLUDE
  "moderate"     → INCLUDE
  "medium"       → INCLUDE
  "medium-low"   → INCLUDE only if bridge_quality contains "strong"
  "low-medium"   → INCLUDE only if bridge_quality contains "strong"
  "low"          → INCLUDE only if bridge_quality contains "strong"
  "rare"         → INCLUDE only if bridge_quality contains "strong"
If the condition is not met → EXCLUDE the key entirely.

Step B2 — SCORING RUBRIC
Assign exactly one integer per key:

  12 = The single role whose bridge_quality field contains 
       "direct target". Exactly ONE key receives 12.

  10 = bridge_quality contains "strong" AND frequency is 
       "medium-high", "high", or "very high"

   9 = bridge_quality contains "strong" AND frequency is 
       "medium-low", "low", "low-medium", or "rare"

   7 = bridge_quality contains "moderate" AND frequency is 
       "medium-high", "high", or "very high"

   6 = bridge_quality contains "moderate" AND frequency is 
       "medium-low", "low", or "rare"

   3 = bridge_quality contains "weak"

  When bridge_quality contains both "moderate" and "strong" 
  (e.g. "moderate-to-strong"), treat as "moderate".

BRIDGE-QUALITY OVERRIDE:
If bridge_quality contains "weak", assign 3 regardless of frequency.

Step B3 — MANDATORY CLOSING ENTRIES (always add, always last)
  "Other adjacent IT": 2
  "Unrelated (sales, legal, manual, etc.)": 0

SECTION 4 — OUTPUT FORMAT AND SCHEMA
Return this exact structure. Field order within each object must 
be preserved.

{
  "candidate_profile": {
    "name": "<string: candidate full name as written in CV>",
    "core_skills": "<string: primary technical skills, comma-separated>",
    "secondary_tools": "<string: supporting tools and platforms, comma-separated>",
    "skill_gaps": "<stringified JSON array: [{\"technology\": \"...\", \"qualifier\": \"...\"}] — ONLY approved qualifier formulas permitted>",
    "home_location": "<string: extracted verbatim from CV — city and region only>",
    "commute_options": "<string: all cities from city_list with train times — home city first>",
    "target_format": "<string: work arrangement and weekly hours from CV or career_target>"
  },
  "role_type_scores": {
    "<role_content_label>": <integer: score per rubric above>,
    "Other adjacent IT": 2,
    "Unrelated (sales, legal, manual, etc.)": 0
  }
}

SECTION 5 — FEW-SHOT EXAMPLE

Input (abbreviated):
<cv_text>
Laura Meier. Frankfurt, Hessen. 
Projects: 
  — E-commerce platform using React, Node.js, PostgreSQL. 
  — REST API service with Node.js and PostgreSQL.
  — Automated testing pipeline with Node.js and Jest.
Technical skills: JavaScript, Node.js, PostgreSQL, Git, Jest.
No mention of Vue.js, Angular, Docker, or Redis.
</cv_text>
<technology_list>
["React", "Node.js", "PostgreSQL", "Vue.js", "Angular", 
 "Docker", "Redis", "Jest"]
</technology_list>
<city_list>
["Frankfurt", "Köln", "Berlin"]
</city_list>
<career_target>Frontend Developer</career_target>
<role_list>
[
  {"label": "Werkstudent Frontend Development", "frequency": "high", 
   "bridge_quality": "strong (direct target)"},
  {"label": "Werkstudent Backend Development", "frequency": "medium-high", 
   "bridge_quality": "strong"},
  {"label": "Werkstudent QA Engineering", "frequency": "medium-low", 
   "bridge_quality": "moderate"}
]
</role_list>

Correct output (skill_gaps section):
"skill_gaps": [
  { "technology": "Vue.js", "qualifier": "no hands-on experience (has used React in the same domain)" },
  { "technology": "Angular", "qualifier": "no hands-on experience (has used React in the same domain)" },
  { "technology": "Docker", "qualifier": "no hands-on experience" },
  { "technology": "Redis", "qualifier": "no hands-on experience" }
]
Note: React, Node.js, PostgreSQL, Jest are NOT in skill_gaps because 
the CV shows hands-on experience with all of them.

Correct output (commute_options section):
"commute_options": "Frankfurt (~0h, home city) | Köln (~1h by train) | Berlin (~4h by train, occasional-only)"

Correct output (role_type_scores section):
"role_type_scores": {
  "Frontend Development": 12,
  "Backend Development": 10,
  "QA Engineering": 6,
  "Other adjacent IT": 2,
  "Unrelated (sales, legal, manual, etc.)": 0
}

SECTION 6 — ANTI-PATTERNS (what NOT to do, with reason)

ANTI-PATTERN 1 — Wrong skill_gaps qualifier:
BAD:  { "technology": "Vue.js", "qualifier": "no hands-on experience 
       (has React background, which provides a conceptual foundation)" }
WHY:  Conceptual foundation language is explicitly forbidden.
GOOD: { "technology": "Vue.js", "qualifier": "no hands-on experience 
       (has used React in the same domain)" }

ANTI-PATTERN 2 — Contract type in role key:
BAD:  { "Praktikum Frontend Development": 12, 
        "Werkstudent Frontend Development": 10 }
WHY:  These are the same role content. Merge into one key.
GOOD: { "Frontend Development": 12 }

ANTI-PATTERN 3 — Multiple values of 12:
BAD:  { "Frontend Development": 12, "Backend Development": 12 }
WHY:  Exactly one key may receive 12.
GOOD: { "Frontend Development": 12, "Backend Development": 10 }

ANTI-PATTERN 4 — Omitting cities from commute_options:
BAD:  "commute_options": "Frankfurt (~0h, home city)"
      [when city_list also contains Köln and Berlin]
WHY:  Every city in <city_list> must appear. No city may be omitted.
GOOD: "commute_options": "Frankfurt (~0h, home city) | 
       Köln (~1h by train) | Berlin (~4h by train, occasional-only)"

ANTI-PATTERN 5 — Text outside the JSON:
BAD:  "Here is the extracted profile:\n{ ... }"
WHY:  Downstream parsing treats the raw response as JSON. Any prefix 
      breaks parsing.
GOOD: { ... }  [JSON starts at character 0]

SECTION 7 — FINAL REMINDER OF CRITICAL RULES [re-read before generating output]
✔ Output starts with { and ends with } — nothing else.
✔ skill_gaps qualifiers use ONLY the two approved formulas. Zero exceptions.
✔ role_type_scores has EXACTLY ONE value of 12.
✔ "Other adjacent IT" and "Unrelated (sales, legal, manual, etc.)" are present.
✔ skill_gaps: every technology in <technology_list> was searched against 
  <cv_text> — including name variants — and removed if found anywhere, 
  regardless of proficiency level.
✔ role_type_scores: every key derived from <role_list> had contract-type 
  words stripped before writing.
✔ commute_options includes every city from <city_list>. Home city appears 
  first. Occasional-only flag applies ONLY to cities STRICTLY GREATER 
  than 2 hours.
✔ home_location contains only what is explicitly written in <cv_text>.
✔ core_skills contains only items from <technology_list>.
